new.title: Eat under the beams at Am Knipp, an inn since 1698
new.desc: Am Knipp on Bergdriesch has been feeding Aachen since 1698, which makes it the oldest restaurant in town. Inside it still looks like an old Öcher pub, with dark beams and long tables for more than 200 guests, and regional cooking on the plates.
new.tip: It only opens in the evening, from 17:30, and stays shut on Monday and Tuesday. In summer ask for the beer garden under its open canopy, and book ahead at weekends.

new.title: Squeeze into the Postwagen on the corner of the Rathaus
new.desc: A little wooden house clings to the corner of the town hall right on the Markt. It once served as a post station and later became a restaurant, and today its 80 seats sit among old walls and warm wood, with down-to-earth regional dishes on the menu.
new.tip: Ask for a window seat looking onto the market square when you book. It is a good place to try Rhineland classics after a visit to the Coronation Hall next door.

new.title: See Dürer prints in a Venetian-style villa
new.desc: The Suermondt-Ludwig-Museum was founded in 1883 and named after the industrialist and collector Barthold Suermondt. Since 1901 it has filled the Villa Cassalette, whose facade copies the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice, with painting and sculpture from the 12th to the 18th century, stained glass, and prints by Dürer, Rembrandt and Goya.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and only opens in the afternoon on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. The stained glass is easy to miss, so look for it before you leave.

new.title: Size up the mighty Marschiertor
new.desc: The southern gate of Aachen's outer wall was begun around 1257 and finished shortly after 1300, and it counts among the most powerful city gates still standing in Western Europe. Over the centuries it has been an arsenal, a storeroom, a homeless shelter and a youth hostel. Since 1964 the carnival guard Oecher Penn has had its headquarters inside.
new.tip: Walk through the passage and look back from Franzstraße to take in its full bulk. It is five minutes on foot from the main station, so it fits neatly at the start or end of a day.

new.title: Stand in three countries at the Dreiländerpunkt
new.desc: On the Vaalserberg, about 5 km from the centre of Aachen, Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium meet at a single point. From 1839 to 1919 a fourth territory touched here too, the tiny neutral zone of Moresnet. The hilltop is also the highest point of the European Netherlands at 322 metres.
new.tip: Walk up through the woods from Vaalserquartier rather than driving round to the Dutch car park. On top you can climb the Belgian Baudouin Tower or get lost in the hedge maze, which takes about 45 minutes to solve.

new.title: Follow the smell of coffee to the Maassen roastery
new.desc: On Stadtstraße in Monschau the Maassen family has roasted coffee since 1862, when Wilhelm Maassen began refining the craft. His great-great-grandsons run the roasting house today, in the middle of the half-timbered old town.
new.tip: Step inside to buy a bag of freshly roasted beans to take home. Small groups can book a guided tour with a tasting by phone.

new.title: Fill a basket at the Düren weekly market
new.desc: Three mornings a week the Marktplatz in the middle of Düren fills with market stalls. The Wochenmarkt runs on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays and is where the town does its shopping and its chatting.
new.tip: It starts at 7:00 from April to September and at 8:00 from October to March, and packs up at 13:30. Come before eleven for the best choice.

new.title: Face a dark chapter at Vogelsang
new.desc: High above the Urft reservoir the Nazi party built a huge training school for its future elite from 1934, designed by the Cologne architect Clemens Klotz. After the war it was a Belgian army camp until 2005 and it only opened to the public in 2006. Today a permanent exhibition explains how the regime tried to shape a master race here, and the Eifel national park centre shares the complex.
new.tip: Allow at least half a day. The grounds and the view over the lake are worth a walk in themselves, and the 48 metre tower can be climbed for a fee.

new.title: Climb to Burg Monschau above the slate roofs
new.desc: The castle above Monschau was first recorded in 1217 and was shelled and plundered by the troops of Emperor Charles V in 1543. In 1836 its owners took the roofs off to dodge a building tax and it fell into ruin, until the town bought it in 1900. The rebuilt main hall has been a youth hostel since 1929, and in 1971 Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the castle in fabric.
new.tip: The steep climb from the old town is short and rewards you with a fine view over the Rur and the roofs. In summer the upper courtyard hosts open-air concerts, including the Monschau Klassik festival.

new.title: Walk or cycle to the Urft dam
new.desc: When it went into service in 1905 the Urft dam was the largest in Europe. Planned by the Aachen professor Otto Intze, the stone wall stands 58 metres tall and 226 metres long, and you can stroll across the top with the reservoir on one side and the drop on the other. Cars cannot drive up to it, which keeps the valley quiet.
new.tip: The lakeside path from the Paulushofdamm car park near Rurberg is the classic way in, and the Rursee boats also stop at the dam. The Urftseemauer inn at the northern end is the place for a break.

new.title: Let the forest run wild on the Kermeter
new.desc: The Kermeter ridge is the core of the Eifel national park and one of the largest unbroken broadleaf forests in the Rhineland, with beeches more than 200 years old. From the Kermeter car park on the L15 a 4.7 km network of gentle paths leads to the Hirschley viewpoint, about 475 metres up, with the Rursee below. The paths are barrier-free, with benches about every 250 metres.
new.tip: Add the Wilder Weg, a 1.5 km trail that starts on a wooden boardwalk and has ten hands-on stations about how a forest becomes wilderness again. Weekday mornings are the quietest.
